title: The Bookkeeper Who Bought an Industry
book: Titan: The Life of John D. Rockefeller, Sr.
author: Ron Chernow
wiifm: Yesterday Peter Thiel argued that the only businesses worth building are the ones that escape competition. Today you watch a real man do it, for forty years, with a ledger and very few scruples. John D. Rockefeller started as a sixteen-year-old clerk on sixteen dollars a month and finished as the richest man in modern history. Ron Chernow's biography shows exactly how: obsessive unit costing, control of the bottleneck, cash held for bad times, and some methods that were indefensible then and illegal now. You will leave knowing which parts to copy and which to never touch.

b: John Davison Rockefeller was born on the eighth of July 1839 in a small farmhouse in Richford, in upstate New York. He was the second of six children, and the eldest son. His parents could hardly have been more different.

His mother, Eliza Davison, was a strict, devout Baptist who ran the household on proverbs. Willful waste makes woeful want was one of them. She taught her children to save, to tithe, and to keep their feelings to themselves.

His father, William Avery Rockefeller, was a travelling salesman of patent medicines who called himself a doctor, wore fine clothes, played the fiddle and was absent for months at a time. Neighbours called him Devil Bill. He was later indicted for rape in 1849, though never tried, and the family moved in a hurry. Most extraordinary of all, from the 1850s he lived a double life as Dr William Levingston, with a second wife named Margaret Allen, while still married to Eliza. John's family kept the secret for decades. A newspaper finally uncovered it in 1908.

One famous line is often quoted: that the father cheated his own sons whenever he could, to make them sharp. It comes from a single second-hand report, so treat it carefully. What is not in doubt is the shape it left. A boy raised by a charming, unreliable, mostly absent father became a man defined by secrecy, self-control and a total refusal to depend on anyone.

As a boy John raised turkeys, sold them, and lent the proceeds to a local farmer at seven per cent interest. When he got his money back with the interest, he said later, he realised he could make money work for him rather than the other way round.
ch.cap: Young John lends his turkey money at seven per cent

b: In 1853 the family settled near Cleveland, Ohio, a booming lake port. John went to high school there and then took a short course in bookkeeping at a commercial college. In the late summer of 1855, aged sixteen, he went looking for work.

He made a list of the most respectable firms in the city, railways, banks and wholesalers, and called on them in turn, six days a week. When he got to the end of the list, he started again. He did not ask for a particular job. He asked whether they needed a bookkeeper. After about six weeks, on the twenty-sixth of September 1855, a firm of produce merchants called Hewitt and Tuttle said yes. He started that morning without asking about pay. The wage was settled later at about sixteen dollars a month.
He celebrated that date for the rest of his life. He called it Job Day, and he marked it more warmly than his own birthday, well into his nineties.

From the start he kept a small notebook he called Ledger A, in which he recorded every cent he earned and spent. He kept it for the rest of his life and treated it almost like a holy relic. He also gave money away from his very first wages, about six per cent at sixteen and ten per cent by the time he was twenty, as a Baptist tithe. Chernow's insight is that the two habits were really one habit. The ledger and the tithe were both refusals to let money be vague.

The point of the ledger is not thrift. A person who records everything eventually knows things that people who record nothing can only feel. That precision would become the foundation of the largest fortune of the age.
ch.cap: On Job Day, Hewitt and Tuttle finally say yes

b: In 1859, aged nineteen, Rockefeller left Hewitt and Tuttle and went into the produce trade with a partner, an Englishman named Maurice Clark. That same August, in Titusville, Pennsylvania, a man named Edwin Drake struck oil by drilling, and a rush began. In 1863 the partners, with a chemist called Samuel Andrews, built a small oil refinery in Cleveland on the side.

Rockefeller quickly came to believe that oil, not groceries, was the future. Clark thought it a dangerous gamble. They quarrelled, and early in 1865 Clark threatened to break up the partnership, assuming his cautious young partner would back down.

Instead they agreed to auction the refinery between themselves, privately, on the spot. Bidding started at five hundred dollars. It climbed past forty thousand, past fifty, past seventy, well beyond what either man obviously had. Clark went to seventy-two thousand. Rockefeller said seventy-two thousand five hundred. Clark said he would go no higher, and that the business was Rockefeller's. Rockefeller had arranged the money from his bankers within days.

He called it the day that determined his career. There are two lessons in it. He had already decided what he believed about the industry, so when the moment came he was not calculating, he was acting. And his reputation for caution was itself an asset, because his opponent never imagined he would bid so high.

A year earlier, in 1864, he had married Laura Celestia Spelman, known as Cettie, a schoolteacher and committed campaigner against slavery and drink. Their marriage lasted fifty years, and she was the steady, private centre of his life.
ch.cap: Rockefeller outbids Clark: seventy-two thousand five hundred

ch.h: A terrible business, and a choke point
b: To understand what Rockefeller did, you need to see how awful the oil business was in the 1860s. Anyone with a lease and a drill could produce oil, so production swung wildly, and the price swung with it, from over ten dollars a barrel to under a dollar and back. Refineries were cheap to build, so hundreds sprang up. Fortunes were made and lost within months. In Adam Smith's terms, it was a market of savage competition where prices kept crashing below the cost of production.

Rockefeller's first strategic insight was to stay out of drilling for many years. Drilling was a lottery. You could not control where the oil was, how much came up or what it would be worth. Refining and transport, on the other hand, were choke points. Only a few railway lines ran from the Pennsylvania oil fields to the cities and ports, and whoever controlled the flow through them could control the industry, whoever owned the wells.

On the tenth of January 1870 he and his partners, including Henry Flagler, Samuel Andrews and his brother William, incorporated the Standard Oil Company of Ohio. The name was a promise: oil of a standard, dependable quality, in an industry where cheap kerosene sometimes exploded in people's lamps.
It was Peter Thiel's strategy a century and a half early. Find the narrowest point in the system, dominate it, and let everyone else fight over the rest.
ch.cap: Countless derricks, but only a few railway lines out

b: Before the famous ruthlessness came arithmetic, pursued to an almost obsessive degree.

Standard Oil found that barrels bought from coopers cost around two dollars and a half each. So it bought its own oak forests, cut its own staves and dried them in kilns before shipping, because dry wood is lighter and cheaper to move. It built its own barrels for less than half the price. Then it built its own wagons and warehouses, bought its own tank cars, laid its own pipelines and eventually ran its own ships. Each step removed a supplier's profit and, just as important, removed a supplier's power to squeeze him.

The best known story is small enough to be a parable. Watching a machine seal five-gallon tins of kerosene for export, Rockefeller asked how many drops of solder it used on each can. Forty, he was told. Had anyone tried thirty-eight? Nobody had. They tried it, and some cans leaked. They tried thirty-nine, and none did. One drop per can sounds like nothing, but Standard sealed millions of cans, and the saving ran year after year. It was worth a great deal of money for a question that cost nothing to ask. He could ask it only because he knew exactly what a can cost.

The same thinking ran through what other refiners threw away. Many of them wanted only kerosene for lamps and poured much of the rest of the crude into rivers. Standard turned the waste into paraffin wax, lubricating oils, petroleum jelly, naphtha and, in time, hundreds of products. This is a different skill from cutting costs. Cutting shrinks a business towards its floor. Turning waste into products raises the ceiling, and it can only be done by someone who has looked closely enough to know what is being thrown away.
ch.cap: Rockefeller asks: has anyone tried thirty-eight drops?

b: This is the part that made him hated, and it is worth understanding precisely, because most accounts blur it.

Railway rebates were normal at the time. A big shipper promised steady volume, and the railway gave him a discount off the published rate, because regular traffic is cheaper to run. That was ordinary commerce. The South Improvement Company of 1872 went much further. It was a company chartered in Pennsylvania in which Rockefeller and Flagler joined a few other refiners and the bosses of the great railways. The deal had three parts.

First, members got rebates. On a barrel of crude carried from the oil regions to New York, for example, the published rate was two dollars fifty-six cents, and members would get one dollar and six cents of it back. Second, and this is the part that still shocks, the railways would also pay the members a drawback on every barrel shipped by their competitors. Your rival ships oil, and you are paid for it. Third, the railways would give members detailed reports on their rivals' shipments: where they went, when, and at what price.
Think about what that does. Your competitor cannot undercut you, cannot outrun you and cannot hide from you. Every barrel he sells helps fund your expansion.

Word leaked in February 1872 and the oil regions erupted. Producers held mass meetings and organised a boycott. On the twenty-fifth of March the railways cancelled the contracts, and on the second of April Pennsylvania repealed the company's charter. The scheme never actually operated. But in the weeks while the threat hung in the air, Rockefeller called on his Cleveland rivals one by one. In under two months, Chernow writes, he absorbed twenty-two of his twenty-six Cleveland competitors. The scheme died. The consolidation it made possible did not.
ch.cap: Rockefeller calls on his Cleveland rivals, one by one

b: The way he bought his rivals was more interesting than either his admirers or his enemies allowed. He did not usually threaten. He explained, like a man doing you a favour, that competition was ruining everyone, that consolidation was coming, and that he was inviting you to join. He offered to buy your refinery for cash or for shares in Standard Oil.

Those who trusted him and took shares generally became far richer than their own refineries could ever have made them. A number of Cleveland families made fortunes this way. Those who distrusted him took cash, often at a low valuation, and watched from outside. The offer was real. It was also made under conditions of hopelessness that he had helped create. Both things are true, which is why he remains so hard to judge.

Secrecy was part of the machine. Standard used code names in telegrams, secretly owned refiners who still traded as independents, and gathered intelligence on rivals constantly. Rockefeller also kept the company's finances strong, with large cash reserves and little reliance on banks. When prices collapsed and rivals ran out of money, he was often the only buyer in the market, and he paid prices set by their desperation.

By the end of the 1870s Standard refined around ninety per cent of America's oil. In 1882 its web of companies was reorganised as the Standard Oil Trust, with nine trustees controlling about forty firms, a legal device to get round rules that stopped a company in one state from owning one in another. When Ohio's courts attacked the trust in 1892, the structure moved, and by 1899 Standard Oil of New Jersey sat on top as a holding company.
ch.cap: A rival refiner chooses: Standard Oil cash or shares

b: The reckoning came from someone who had grown up in the wreckage. Ida Tarbell was raised in the Pennsylvania oil regions, and her father, Franklin, was an independent oil producer and tank maker whose business suffered badly in the struggles of the 1870s. Between 1902 and 1904 she published a nineteen-part History of the Standard Oil Company in McClure's Magazine, later a book.

It was one of the most influential pieces of journalism ever written, and it was meticulously sourced from court records, testimony and documents. It was also personal, which its admirers sometimes forget. Her brother William was an executive at a rival firm, the Pure Oil Company, and helped her with information. President Theodore Roosevelt later used the word muckrakers for journalists like her. They took it as a badge of honour.

The federal government sued Standard Oil in 1906 under the Sherman Antitrust Act. On the fifteenth of May 1911 the Supreme Court ordered the company broken up. The opinion, written by Chief Justice Edward White, set out the rule of reason, that the law forbids only unreasonable restraints of trade. Standard was split into thirty-four companies. Their descendants include Exxon, Mobil, Chevron and Amoco.

Then came the twist. Rockefeller owned about a quarter of the shares in every one of the successor companies. As the market valued them separately, their prices soared, and his fortune roughly doubled. By 1913 it was put at about nine hundred million dollars, which Chernow and others calculate as over two per cent of the entire American economy. On that measure, no modern fortune comes close.
ch.cap: Ida Tarbell builds her case against Standard Oil

ch.h: Ludlow, the giving, and the bill
b: The defence of Rockefeller is strong and you should know it. Across his decades in charge, the price of kerosene fell sharply and its quality rose. Before Standard, lamp oil was costly and sometimes deadly. Afterwards, ordinary households could afford safe light. Standard's share was also shrinking before the courts acted, as new fields in Texas and rivals such as Gulf and Texaco grew. Consumers did well.

But his competitors were destroyed by methods that were not competition in any honest sense. A drawback is not efficiency. It is a private tax on other people's trade. And in April 1914, at a Colorado mining company largely owned by the Rockefellers and overseen by his son, a long strike ended when the National Guard attacked a tent colony at Ludlow. Around twenty people died, including women and children, most of them in a fire. The family's response was to hire Ivy Lee, who more or less invented modern corporate public relations.

Rockefeller gave money away with the same system he used for refining. He founded the University of Chicago in 1890 and the Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research in 1901, and his foundations transformed medicine and education. One campaign against hookworm in the American South largely cleared a parasite that had sapped the health of millions. In his lifetime he gave away roughly five hundred and thirty million dollars.
He spent his last years playing golf, handing out shiny dimes to strangers, and hoping to reach a hundred. He died at Ormond Beach, Florida, on the twenty-third of May 1937, aged ninety-seven.

Chernow's verdict is that he was neither the saint his church admired nor the monster Tarbell drew, but something harder to accept: a man of real principle who decided early that the rules governing his soul did not govern his business. For a business owner, the lesson is to copy his precision, his costing and his cash reserves, and leave the drawbacks alone. Tomorrow, the question changes from how to build wealth to how not to lose it.
ch.cap: Aged Rockefeller hands a shiny dime to a child

take: Rockefeller knew what everything cost to the cent. Work out the fully loaded cost of delivering one unit of what you sell, such as one lead, one case or one application, broken down step by step.
Find a step that is both costly and frequent and ask the smallest reduction that would still work. Test it properly on a sample, as he tested thirty-eight drops before settling on thirty-nine.
He stayed out of drilling and controlled refining and transport. Identify the narrowest point between you and your customers and make sure you are not at someone else's mercy there.
Standard sold what rivals poured into rivers. Look at what your business discards, such as unconverted leads, declined applications or unused content, and ask whether any of it can be sold or reused.
He won the refinery because his thinking was already done. Settle your view on the big strategic questions in calm times, so you can act fast when the moment comes.
His reserves let him buy when rivals were desperate. Decide what you would buy if a competitor got into trouble, and size your reserve to that, not just to surviving a bad month.
Some advantages are not worth having
The drawback was a private tax on rivals and later became illegal. In a regulated business especially, an edge that would embarrass you if published is a liability, not an asset.
Ludlow and Tarbell defined the family for generations, despite enormous philanthropy. How you win counts as much as winning.
recall: What was the difference between a rebate and a drawback in the 1872 scheme?

A rebate was a discount off the published rate for members' own shipments, such as one dollar six cents back on a two dollar fifty-six crude rate to New York. A drawback was a further payment to members on every barrel their competitors shipped. The first made Rockefeller cheaper; the second made his rivals finance him.
Why did Rockefeller avoid drilling for so long?

Production was a lottery: anyone could drill, output and prices swung violently and no producer had control. Refining and transport were choke points with few routes to market, so controlling them meant controlling the industry.
What happened in Cleveland in early 1872?

While the South Improvement scheme threatened rival refiners, Rockefeller bought out most of them, absorbing twenty-two of his twenty-six Cleveland competitors in under two months. The scheme itself was killed by public outrage by early April, but the consolidation stuck.
What choice did Rockefeller offer the refiners he bought, and why did it matter?
Cash or Standard Oil shares. Those who took shares often became far richer than their refineries could have made them; those who took cash sold cheaply and gained nothing more.
What happened when Standard Oil was broken up in 1911?

The Supreme Court split it into thirty-four companies, setting out the rule of reason. Rockefeller owned about a quarter of each, their shares soared, and his fortune roughly doubled to about nine hundred million dollars by 1913.
note: Facts follow Chernow's Titan, including Job Day, Ledger A, the 1865 auction, the solder story and the figure of twenty-two of twenty-six Cleveland refiners absorbed in 1872. The South Improvement rates of two dollars fifty-six with a one dollar six rebate applied to crude shipped from the oil regions to New York, as Tarbell records, not to Cleveland. The line about William Rockefeller cheating his sons rests on a single second-hand source. Ludlow death tolls vary between accounts, and the comparison of the 1913 fortune to American GDP is an estimate.

biz: Rockefeller knew the cost of a single can to the cent. Work out the fully loaded cost of one completed secured loan: ad spend, call time, WhatsApp time, document chasing, compliance checks and lender liaison, divided by completions. Do the same for one debt advice case. Then ask the solder question of one costly, frequent step, such as an extra form field or a repeat document request, and test a small change on a sample of cases before rolling it out. Measure completion rate and complaints alongside cost, so savings never come at the customer's expense.
Turn waste into help, never into pressure

Standard sold what rivals poured into rivers. Your waste is enquiries that do not proceed: declined applications, homeowners who would be unwise to secure more debt, people clearly in financial difficulty. Rather than chasing them or passing on their data, build a clear consent based route: explain plainly why a loan may not be right, signpost free advice such as MoneyHelper, and offer a Debt Support Direct appointment only where it genuinely fits and the customer agrees. Record outcomes and check for vulnerability. Rockefeller's drawback is the reminder: an edge that would embarrass you if published is a liability.
connects: Rockefeller controlling refining and transport while everyone else fought over drilling is Thiel's strategy of dominating the choke point and escaping competition, a century and a half early.
Rockefeller, like Machiavelli's prince, kept one set of rules for his private soul and another for his business, and was judged by history on the methods as much as the results.
Rockefeller's lifelong ledger and large cash reserves show the Psychology of Money idea that saving and staying solvent are what let you act when others are forced to sell.
recap:
John D. Rockefeller was the son of a charming fraud. His father sold patent medicines, called himself a doctor, vanished for months, and secretly kept a second wife under another name. His mother taught him to save, to give to the church, and to keep his feelings to himself. The boy who came out of that house trusted nobody and recorded everything.

At sixteen, in Cleveland, he walked from one respectable firm to the next asking for work, and when he reached the end of his list he started again. After six weeks a produce merchant took him on. He celebrated that day, which he called Job Day, more warmly than his birthday for the rest of his life. From his first wages he kept a small notebook of every cent in and out, and gave part of his pay away.

The first big idea is precision. A person who records everything ends up knowing what others can only guess. Watching a machine seal kerosene cans with forty drops of solder, he asked whether thirty-eight would do. Thirty-eight leaked. Thirty-nine did not. Across millions of cans, one drop paid handsomely.

The second idea is to make your big decisions before the moment arrives. When his partner tried to bully him by threatening to break up their firm, Rockefeller bought him out at auction for seventy-two thousand five hundred dollars, because he had already decided that oil was the future.

The third is to control the choke point. Drilling was a lottery, so he stayed out of it and dominated refining and transport, owning barrels, tank cars, pipelines and ships, and selling the waste that others poured into rivers.

The fourth is cash. Strong reserves meant that when prices collapsed he was often the only buyer left, paying prices set by other men's desperation.

The fifth is the warning. In eighteen seventy-two a secret railway scheme would have paid his group a share on every barrel their rivals shipped, and handed them their rivals' shipping records. It was exposed and cancelled, but in the panic he swallowed twenty-two of his twenty-six Cleveland competitors. By the end of the decade Standard Oil refined about nine tenths of America's oil. A journalist named Ida Tarbell, whose father had suffered in those wars, laid the methods bare, and in nineteen eleven the Supreme Court broke the company up. His shares in the pieces made him richer still, and he gave away more than half a billion dollars.

Copy the ledger, the costing and the cash, and leave the secret deals alone, because how you win is remembered as long as the winning.
